osi7.heading: OSI Layer 7 (Application)
osi7.body: SOAP operates entirely within the Application Layer. While it often uses HTTP as its transport mechanism (treating HTTP like a lower-level network protocol), it can conceptually sit on top of any Layer 7 protocol, including SMTP or FTP. The heavy lifting of security (WS-Security) and routing (WS-Addressing) happens here, inside the XML envelope.

proxy.heading: The Role of the Proxy
proxy.body: A key difference between SOAP and REST is the strong typing provided by WSDL (Web Services Description Language). The WSDL defines the exact shape of the XML required. Development tools use this to generate a "Proxy" class, allowing developers to call a remote API exactly like a local function, hiding all the XML serialization complexity.

proxyPattern.heading: The Proxy & Facade Pattern Abstraction
proxyPattern.intro: SOAP inherently relies on the Proxy Pattern, which acts much like a Facade to completely abstract the complexity of network calls away from the developer. The foundation of this is the WSDL, which IDEs use to auto-generate Client Proxies (stubs).

developerView.heading: 1. The Developer's View (The Facade)
developerView.body: To the developer writing the application logic, calling the remote server looks exactly like calling a local method on a local object. They do not write HTTP clients or parse XML.

hiddenComplexity.heading: 2. The Hidden Complexity
hiddenComplexity.body: When the developer calls that method, the generated Proxy intercepts it and handles massive complexity behind the scenes:
bullets: Serialization: Converts native objects into XML structure.
Envelope Construction: Wraps payload in SOAP Headers/Body.
Network Transport: Opens HTTP/TCP connections and sends data.
Error Translation: Parses returning XML and translates SOAP Faults into native language Exceptions.

leakyAbstraction.heading: The "Leaky Abstraction" Drawback
leakyAbstraction.body: While this abstraction enables rapid development, it completely hides the network. Because remote calls look identical to local method calls, developers can easily forget they incur significant network latency (e.g., carelessly placing a proxy call inside a tight for loop), leading to severe performance bottlenecks known as the N+1 problem.

tooling.heading: Tooling: Generating Proxies
tooling.intro: Because the WSDL acts as a strict, machine-readable contract, developers rarely write the SOAP XML or the network routing code manually. Instead, they rely on language-specific tools to generate the local Proxy classes (stubs) and data models.

AppClient.title: 1. Client Application
AppClient.overview: The originating software system that needs to consume a remote SOAP service to fetch data or trigger an action.
AppClient.interaction: Passes arguments to the locally instantiated Proxy class.
AppClient.branching: If the data provided to the method is invalid locally, the application throws an exception before the network is even engaged.

Proxy.title: 2. Client Proxy / Stub
Proxy.overview: A piece of code acting as a local representative of the remote service, intercepting method calls and packaging the parameters for transmission.
Proxy.interaction: Takes language-specific objects and passes them to the Serialization framework.
Proxy.branching: The proxy enforces type safety. If the developer tries to call a method not defined in the WSDL contract, it fails (at compile time for Java/.NET, or runtime for Python).

Serialize.title: 3. Serialize to SOAP Message
Serialize.overview: The framework's engine converts the application's native in-memory objects into a structured SOAP XML document format according to XML Schema rules.
Serialize.interaction: Passes the resulting raw XML string to the Transport Protocol layer.
Serialize.branching: If serialization fails (e.g., encountering a circular reference), a runtime serialization exception is thrown.

TransportProtocol.title: 4. Transport Protocol
TransportProtocol.overview: The Layer 7 delivery mechanism used to transmit the SOAP message over the network. HTTP and HTTPS are the most common.
TransportProtocol.interaction: Wraps the SOAP message in an HTTP Request (e.g., POST with a SOAPAction header) and hands it to the OS networking stack.
TransportProtocol.branching: If the network is unreachable, it throws a Timeout/Connection Exception back to the client application.
TransportProtocol.devImpact: Devs configure endpoint URLs, timeouts, SSL/TLS certificates, and transport-level authentication.

Envelope.title: SOAP Envelope
Envelope.overview: The mandatory root element of a SOAP message. It encapsulates the entire payload, defining the XML document explicitly as a SOAP message.
Envelope.interaction: Contains exactly two child elements: an optional Header and a mandatory Body.
Envelope.branching: If the Envelope namespace is unrecognized, the server immediately rejects the request without processing it further.
Envelope.devImpact: Devs rarely construct this manually. It defines the SOAP version (1.1 vs 1.2), which dictates specific namespaces and content types.

Header.title: SOAP Header
Header.overview: An optional XML block used for routing and meta-information. It is famous for housing WS-* specifications, such as WS-Security.
Header.interaction: Read by server-side interceptors before the main Body is parsed or business logic is executed.
Header.branching: Headers can have a mustUnderstand="1" attribute. If the server does not know how to process it, it aborts and returns a SOAP Fault.
Header.devImpact: This is where SOAP complexity peaks. Devs write middleware to inject security tokens, transaction IDs, or custom tracing IDs into the header before transmission.

Body.title: SOAP Body
Body.overview: The required main payload. It contains the XML data representing the specific method being called and its parameters.
Body.interaction: Extracted by the server parser and handed directly to the business logic layer.
Body.branching: If processing is successful, it returns a standard response Body. If an error occurs, it returns a Body containing a standard soap:Fault element.
Body.devImpact: This represents the core domain data. The structure here maps exactly to the request/response models the developer works with in their application code.

Fault.title: SOAP Fault
Fault.overview: A standardized error block nested inside the Body. It provides structured error reporting containing a fault code, a human-readable fault string, and technical details.
Fault.interaction: Returns backwards through the network to inform the Client Application of the failure.
Fault.branching: A Fault dictates that normal execution failed. It immediately branches the client application into its error-handling flow.

TCP.title: OSI Layers 1-4
TCP.overview: The lower-level network stack that breaks the HTTP payload into packets, establishes the connection across the network (TCP Handshake).
TCP.interaction: Carries the payload across switches, routers, and firewalls to the Server Transport listener.
TCP.branching: If packets are lost, TCP automatically retries. If the connection drops entirely, a Connection Reset (RST) is passed up.
TCP.devImpact: Mostly an infrastructure/DevOps concern. However, devs may need to debug this layer using Wireshark if there are TLS cipher mismatches.

Deserialize.title: 6. Parse SOAP XML
Deserialize.overview: The server-side SOAP engine reads the raw XML string and translates it back into native server-side memory objects.
Deserialize.interaction: Sends the parsed objects to the Validation layer.
Deserialize.branching: If the XML is malformed, the parser throws an immediate fatal error and returns an HTTP 500 or Bad Request Fault.
Deserialize.devImpact: Framework handles this. Devs configure the server-side XML parsers and ensure their endpoint is correctly mapped to the incoming URL route.

Validate.title: 7. WSDL Contract Validation
Validate.overview: The server strictly checks the parsed XML against its XML Schema Definition (XSD). This enforces strong typing and strict structural rules.
Validate.interaction: If valid, triggers the execution of the Application Service Logic.
Validate.branching: If data types are wrong, fields are missing, or extra unauthorized fields exist, it rejects it immediately and generates a validation Fault.
Validate.devImpact: Devs rely on this so they do not have to write manual null checks or type-checking logic in their business code. The schema guarantees the data is exactly the right shape.
